opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that the web was built for humans, and the entire search stack, both the technology and the economics, is optimized around a human sitting in front of a screen with limited time and attention.

Think about what traditional search does. A person types a few keywords, and the engine's job is to return ten blue links ranked so that you'll click on one of them in the next couple of seconds. Everything is tuned for that: short queries, fast results, a page that fits on a screen, and ranking that predicts what a human is likely to click. And the business model follows from that. You monetize attention. Ads sit next to results, and publishers get traffic in return for letting themselves be indexed. That's the bargain that's held the web together for twenty-five years.

Now put an AI agent in that seat instead of a person. The agent doesn't have limited attention in the same way. It can read hundreds of pages. It doesn't want ten links, it wants the right information, often deep, precise, and comprehensive, so it can reason over it and get a task done. Its queries look different too. They can be long, detailed, multi-part, almost like a research brief. And the agent cares about things humans don't think much about, like latency at scale, freshness, how much content you return, in what format, and how cleanly it fits into a context window. So the retrieval problem itself changes. You're no longer optimizing for "what will a person click," you're optimizing for "what does a model need to reason correctly." That means rethinking indexing, ranking, how you extract and package content, really the whole pipeline.

And then the business model breaks, because an agent doesn't look at ads. If the primary consumer of the web is increasingly machines, the attention-based economy doesn't carry over. Which raises a real question for publishers and creators: why would they keep making high-quality content available if the traffic and ad revenue that justified it start going away? If we don't answer that, the open web gets worse, and that's bad for everyone, including the AI systems that depend on it.

So I think you have to rebuild both sides together. On the technology side, search designed from first principles for AI, where quality and depth matter more than a ranked list of clicks. On the economic side, a model where whoever uses the information pays for it directly, and some of that value flows back to the people who create the content. Agents are going to be the biggest users of the web, potentially by orders of magnitude more than humans, and that's a huge opportunity, but only if we build infrastructure that's actually designed for them and an economy that keeps the web healthy.

r001.rationale: The response says agents may use the web “by orders of magnitude more than humans,” but does not clearly specify roughly a thousand times more.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that web search was built for a very specific customer, a human being typing a few words into a box, and almost everything about it, from the ranking to the economics, is shaped around that customer. Agents are a fundamentally different customer, and when the customer changes that much, you can't just bolt a new interface onto the old system.

Start with the technology. A human issues maybe a handful of queries a day, and for each one, you show ten blue links and let the person do the work of clicking, reading, deciding, and refining. The search engine is really optimizing for a tiny slice of the problem, which is getting a person to a reasonable starting point as fast as possible. An agent doesn't want ten links. An agent wants to ask a hundred or a thousand questions in the course of a single task, it wants the actual content and not a snippet, it wants to know what's recent and what's authoritative, and it wants all of that at a latency and cost that makes a thousand calls feasible. It's also totally fine with results that would be terrible for a human, like a long structured dump of everything relevant, because a model can read much more than a person can. So the retrieval problem, the ranking problem, and even what counts as a "result" all look different. We found we had to rethink the index itself, how often it's refreshed, how deep it goes, and what signals matter when the thing consuming the output is a model reasoning over it rather than a person scanning it.

Then there's the business model, and this is the part people underestimate. Search as we've known it is funded by ads, and ads work because a human looks at the page. The entire incentive structure, which is to keep people on the results page and nudge them toward sponsored content, is actively hostile to what an agent needs. An agent doesn't look at ads, and you really don't want a world where the agent's "search results" are quietly biased toward whoever paid the most. That would corrupt the whole thing. So the economics have to flip. The search provider has to make money by being useful to the developer and the agent, which means a straightforward model where you pay for calls and the provider is rewarded for accuracy, freshness, and coverage instead of for engagement. That's a healthier alignment, but it's a completely different company to build, and it's not something an existing ad-driven player can easily pivot to, because every incentive they have points the other way.

And the two problems are tied together. If you're going to charge per call and agents are going to make a thousand calls per task, you have to drive the cost down dramatically, which pushes you back into the technology question. You can't do it with the old architecture and old economics. That's why I think of it as reinventing both at once rather than improving either one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a human’s handful of daily queries with an agent’s hundred or thousand questions in a task, but it does not clearly state that agents will use the web roughly a thousand times more than humans.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental shift is that search has traditionally been built for a person who types a few words, gets a list of links, and then does the work of figuring out the answer. With an AI agent, the consumer of search is software. It might need to make many searches, combine evidence across sources, and use that information to complete a task. So simply giving it the same page of results isn’t necessarily the right interface.

That changes what you optimize for. Can the agent get the information it needs reliably? Is it fresh? Can it trace a claim back to its source? And can it do that with the latency and cost that make sense when search is happening repeatedly inside a larger workflow? Those requirements push you to rethink the system beyond just the presentation of results.

The business model changes for the same reason. The traditional model depends heavily on human attention and advertising. An agent isn’t browsing ads or choosing links in the same way. You need a model where the customer pays for the value of retrieving useful information, and you also need to think about how the people producing that information benefit. Otherwise, you risk building a very useful retrieval system while weakening the ecosystem that supplies its knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response says agents may make many repeated searches, but gives no expectation that they will use the web roughly a thousand times more than humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental shift is that search has historically been built for a human who types a few words, looks at a page of links, and decides what to click. An AI agent needs something different. It might issue many searches to accomplish one task, and it needs information it can actually reason over—relevant content, enough context, and clear sources—rather than a page designed for a person to browse.

That changes the technical problem. You have to think about how an agent expresses what it needs, how you retrieve the right information, and how you deliver it with the latency and reliability that an automated workflow requires. Simply putting an API around the existing search experience doesn't address all of that.

The business model changes for the same reason. Advertising works when you have human attention and clicks. If an agent is doing the searching, those assumptions become much weaker. There's an opportunity to build a model where the customer pays for useful information, and where the people producing that information have an incentive to make it available. The technology and the economics have to work together.

r001.rationale: The response says agents may issue many searches for one task, but does not state or clearly imply roughly a thousand times more web use than humans.
